source.title: Prototype-Based Multiple Instance Learning for Gigapixel Whole Slide Image Classification
source.authors: Su-Su Sun; D. van Midden; Geert Litjens; Christian F. Baumgartner

page_placements.theme: Applied SAE latents are largely but not fully monosemantic; top-activation labels can misstate causal role

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different approach—sparse-autoencoder concept discovery and pathologist assessment—to report how often learned visual concepts are monosemantic and that some SAE neurons remain polysemantic.
record.gate_note: The reported monosemantic-concept percentages and the explicit statement that some SAE neurons remain polysemantic bear on V1. Classification-performance results, artifact-removal results, and SAE hyperparameter choices do not measure polysemanticity and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses a sparse autoencoder, built on the superposition idea, as a tool for concept discovery. The 75% and 86% monosemantic shares evaluate its own SAE latents, not the neurons of an image classifier. The study reports its method's interpretability and classification performance and does not measure how often classifier neurons respond to unrelated inputs. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the SAE learns sparse, human-interpretable pathology concepts. They also say ProtoMIL matches state-of-the-art MIL accuracy and allows intervention on spurious concepts. They note that 'a certain number' of SAE neurons remain polysemantic and leave reducing this to future work, giving no count beyond the 75%/86% monosemantic shares.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an SAE on histopathology image embeddings, selects top-activating patches for interpretation, and asks pathologists to assess concepts; it does not reproduce the original neuron investigation.

fits_no_version.finding: In an SAE trained on CONCH pathology embeddings, one pathologist judged 75% (Camelyon16) and 86% (PANDA) of the 74 activated concepts monosemantic. The authors state that some SAE neurons remain polysemantic but do not quantify this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse-autoencoder latents trained on vision foundation-model embeddings are largely, but not fully, monosemantic.

record.code_released: https://github.com/ss-sun/ProtoMIL (stated as code that will be publicly available)
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (2025)
record.problems: The assessment is reported as a pathologist evaluation, but the text does not state the number of raters or an uncertainty measure. The paper does not quantify the polysemantic concepts or show that their inputs are unrelated.
record.rows_left_out: Classification metrics and concept-intervention results were left out because they do not measure polysemanticity; see Table 1 and Section 3, Evaluations with Intervention on Spurious Concepts.

untested.parts: No classifier or encoder neurons, including raw CONCH units, are examined for responses to unrelated inputs. Only SAE latents are assessed.
Untested: superposition is assumed as the motivation for the SAE, not tested.
Untested: the SAE hyperparameter search (λ1, dhid) does not report polysemanticity by setting.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V1' label is unwarranted. The polysemanticity remark concerns SAE latents from the study's own method, not classifier neurons, and no unrelated-input responses are shown. There is a single unnamed pathologist evaluation. Only 74 of 2048 latents ever activate.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test InceptionV1 or the cited cat-face/car-front/cat-leg neuron, nor whether the remaining polysemantic concepts respond to unrelated inputs.
Language-model MLP neurons and token or context responses.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is sufficient capacity.
No comparison of architectures, activation functions, or regularization settings for their effect on polysemanticity; no test of lowering it without substantial performance loss.
Does not investigate whether specific canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots of one job.
Does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

relation.reason: The SAE/monosemanticity idea is used as a tool. The monosemantic shares evaluate the study's own SAE latents, not neurons of an image classifier or language model.

tranche.reason: The study uses an SAE as a concept-discovery tool and reports only its own method's interpretability and MIL accuracy. It does not measure polysemanticity of classifier or CONCH neurons.

source_check.notes: The 75%/86% measure the study's own SAE latents (d_hid 2048, 74 active), judged by one pathologist, with no raw-neuron baseline and no per-dataset concept counts. They say nothing about polysemantic classifier neurons. The text says only that 'a certain number' of SAE neurons remain polysemantic.

statements.correction: The SAE was trained on frozen CONCH embeddings of patches from both datasets. Per the pathologist's evaluation, 75% of detected concepts on Camelyon16 and 86% on PANDA captured monosemantic pathology features. Separately, 74 concepts were activated in total across the SAE training set (3M Camelyon16 + 4.7M PANDA patches). The per-dataset concept counts are not given.
statements.problem: 75% and 86% are shares of the concepts detected on each dataset, not of the 74. The 74 is the total activated across the whole SAE training set (both datasets). 75% of 74 is not a whole number, so 74 cannot be the denominator. One pathologist is fair ('the pathologist's evaluation').
